Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others
Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
There is something about me that made the event happen

vignette: Carlos had never imagined that a single night on a quiet Main Street could unravel the fabric of his everyday life. He was returning from a late dinner with a client when a sudden burst of shouting erupted between a police officer and a suspect in an alleyway. The officer's shotgun-like burst of light flashed, a bright blue-green sting that turned the suspect's skin a sickly gray. Blood welled from a cut on the suspect's arm, dripping onto the pavement. Carlos felt a sharp jolt in his chest, the metallic taste of fear, and his head began to ache with a pounding that felt like a physical wound. He stared, helpless, at the bruised figure on the curb as the officer shouted orders, and the scene lingered in his mind. That night, as he lay in bed, the image of the visible injuries replayed, and the memory of the victim's frightened eyes haunted him. He felt an acute sense of isolation, as though the world had turned its back on him, and a gnawing belief that something in him had somehow brought this violence to the street. The idea that he might have been complicit, that his mere presence could have sparked the confrontation, settled heavily in his thoughts. The trauma's vivid visual cues, the vivid reminder of the victim's pain, and the physical ache he carried that morning became the triggers that flooded his mind with these negative appraisals: a feeling of being cut off from others, a conviction that his life had lost value, and an intrinsic sense of fault that seemed to hang around his shoulders. When the first night passed, the images did not fade; they seeped into Carlos's daily life. The moment he left his house for work, he hesitated, half-heartedly scanning for unfamiliar surroundings, because the very idea of an unknown place made his throat tighten. Each time he stepped into a new client's office, he felt a cold knot form in his chest. He began to carry a mental map of each room, noting possible exits, and he would pause to look over his shoulder, listening for a hidden danger. This threat-oriented vigilance emerged directly from the weight of his negative appraisals: feeling alone, doubting the worth of his own existence, and believing his mere presence might trigger harm. The need to identify escape routes, to avoid unfamiliar places, and to constantly check behind him became a protective ritual that, paradoxically, deepened his sense of isolation. He could no longer enjoy a simple walk to the coffee shop without first calculating the safest path back. The loop tightened when his threat behaviors began to produce new triggers. While crouching behind a desk to assess the layout of a client's conference room, the sudden sound of footsteps behind him snapped him to a state of hypervigilance, and he perceived the faint echo as a reminder of that night's officer's gunfire. The sight of a colleague's hand gripping a stack of tax documents-a mundane visual-evoked, in Carlos's mind, the sharp blue-green flash that had marked the officer's blast. Each avoidance plan, each check, fed back into his fear of being watched, and the memory of the victim's pain seeped again through every small detail that could be misread as a threat. His isolation grew, and he found himself withdrawing from family dinners, his divorce remaining a closed chapter that he no longer dared to reopen. The avoidance that once felt protective now amplified his sense that life was not worth living. Today, Carlos sits across from his therapist, the same room that holds a framed photo of a happier past. He can no longer attend a client meeting at a new office without a pre-written escape map, and he rarely leaves the safety of his own apartment. He has stopped taking his usual lunch walks because every street corner now looks like an alleyway of potential danger. Sleep has slipped away into restless nights punctuated by dreams of visible injuries and the ringing blue-green light. The weight of these loops has convinced him that he is unworthy of a future that could be threatened again. It was this relentless, sleepless night, coupled with a sense that he could not perform his job without feeling constantly on edge, that finally pushed Carlos to seek help. He fears that he will lose the only remaining sense of stability in his life, yet he hopes that, by unraveling the painful cycle, he might once again feel safe in an unfamiliar world.
